problem: Source says heart and mind were thrilled/astonished but "neither were softened"; "comforted" changes the point (St. John's preaching lacks tenderness, not merely consolation).
new_text: It began calmly—and indeed, in terms of delivery and tone of voice, it remained calm to the end: but a deeply felt, tightly controlled passion soon breathed through the precise words and drove the powerful language. This grew to force—compressed, concentrated, restrained. The heart was stirred, the mind astonished by the preacher's power: neither was softened. Throughout there ran a strange bitterness; an absence of gentle consolation; stern references to Calvinist doctrines—election, predestination, damnation—were frequent; and each mention of these ideas sounded like a sentence of doom pronounced. When he finished, instead of feeling better, calmer, more enlightened by his words, I experienced an inexpressible sadness; for it seemed to me—whether equally so to others I cannot say—that the eloquence I had been hearing had sprung from a depth where stirred dark sediments of disappointment, where troubled currents of unsatisfied yearning and restless ambition flowed. I was certain St. John Rivers—clean-living, conscientious, zealous as he was—had not yet found that peace of God which passes all understanding: he had no more found it, I thought, than I had with my hidden, gnawing grief for my shattered idol and lost paradise—grief I have lately avoided mentioning, but which possessed me and tyrannized over me without mercy.

problem: "the patch of moorish soil" means moorland ground; "boggy ground" introduces a different image.
new_text: "You need not be in any hurry to hear," he said. "Let me be frank: I have nothing attractive or lucrative to suggest. Before I explain, please recall my clear warning that if I helped you, it would be as the blind helping the lame. I am poor; for I find that, when I have paid my father's debts, all the inheritance remaining to me will be this crumbling house, the row of damaged firs behind, and the patch of moorland soil with the yew trees and holly bushes in front. I am obscure: Rivers is an old name; but of the three sole descendants of the line, two earn a dependent's wages among strangers, and the third considers himself an exile from his native land—not only for life but in death. Yes, and deems, and is bound to deem, himself honored by this fate, and aspires only for the day when the cross of separation from earthly ties shall be laid on his shoulders, and when the Head of that Church Militant of whose humblest members he is one shall give the word: 'Rise, follow Me!'"

problem: "the fear of servitude with strangers entered my soul like iron" echoes the biblical "the iron entered into his soul" (Psalm 105:18); "cut deep into my soul" drops the allusion.
new_text: He put the question somewhat hurriedly; he seemed half to expect an indignant, or at least a scornful, rejection of the offer: not knowing all my thoughts and feelings, though guessing some, he could not tell how the prospect would look to me. In truth it was humble—but it was sheltered, and I wanted a safe haven. It was dull—but compared to the life of a governess in a wealthy household, it was independent; and the fear of servitude among strangers entered my soul like iron. It was not ignoble—not unworthy—not intellectually degrading. I made my decision.

problem: "hewers of wood and drawers of water" is a recognizable biblical phrase (Joshua 9:21) flattened to "woodcutters and water-carriers"; also "propensities" (natural inclinations) became "ambitions", narrowing the meaning.
new_text: "I was going to say passionate: but perhaps you would misunderstand the word and be offended. I mean that human bonds and sympathies have a very powerful hold on you. I am sure you cannot long be content to spend your free time in solitude and devote your working hours to monotonous labor completely devoid of stimulation: any more than I can be content," he added with emphasis, "to live here buried in marshland, hemmed in by mountains—my nature, God-given, thwarted; my abilities, heaven-bestowed, paralyzed—rendered useless. You hear how I contradict myself. I, who preached contentment with a humble lot and defended the calling even of hewers of wood and drawers of water in God's service—I, His ordained minister, nearly rave in my restlessness. Well, inclinations and principles must somehow be reconciled."

problem: The proverb "the slip between the cup and the lip" is dropped and replaced by the paraphrase "a last-minute disappointment"; the allusion should stay recognizable.
new_text: At that moment a small event occurred that seemed decreed by fate specifically to confirm the truth of the saying that "misfortunes never come alone," and to add to their troubles the maddening one of the slip between the cup and the lip. St. John passed the window reading a letter. He came in.

problem: Diana's "Amen!" (a pious acceptance, in keeping with the Rivers' religious register) is secularized to "So be it!".
new_text: "Amen! We can still live," said Diana at last.

problem: "a momentary damp is cast on the spirits" — the qualifier "momentary" (the disappointment is brief) is dropped.
new_text: "Jane, you will wonder at us and our mysteries," she said, "and think us hard-hearted for not being more upset at the death of so close a relative as an uncle; but we have never met him or known him. He was my mother's brother. My father and he quarreled long ago. It was on his advice that my father risked most of his money in the speculation that ruined him. Bitter accusations flew between them: they parted in anger and were never reconciled. My uncle went on to more successful ventures: it appears he accumulated a fortune of twenty thousand pounds. He never married and had no close family but ourselves and one other person, no more closely related than we are. My father always clung to the hope that he would make amends for his error by leaving his money to us; that letter informs us that he has left every penny to the other relative, except for thirty guineas to be split between St. John, Diana, and Mary Rivers, for the purchase of three mourning rings. He had every right, of course, to do as he pleased: and yet receiving such news dampens the spirits for a moment. Mary and I would have counted ourselves rich with a thousand pounds each; and to St. John such a sum would have been valuable for the good it would have enabled him to do."

problem: "too far to leave hope of ultimate restoration thither" means too far to hope he could ever return to the right path; "his eventual return" is ambiguous (could read as his return to Jane).
new_text: While I looked, I thought myself happy, and was surprised to find myself before long weeping—and why? For the fate that had torn me from my master: for him I was never to see again; for the desperate grief and destructive fury—consequences of my departure—that might now, perhaps, be dragging him from the right path, too far to leave any hope of his ever finding his way back to it. At this thought, I turned my face from the lovely evening sky and the lonely vale of Morton—I say lonely, for in the stretch of it visible to me there was no building except the church and the parsonage, half-hidden in trees, and, at the very far end, the roof of Vale Hall, where the rich Mr. Oliver and his daughter lived. I covered my eyes and leaned my head against the stone doorframe; but soon a slight sound near the little gate that separated my tiny garden from the meadow beyond made me look up. A dog—old Carlo, Mr. Rivers' pointer, as I saw at once—was pushing the gate with his nose, and St. John himself leaned on it with folded arms; his brow furrowed, his gaze stern almost to displeasure, fixed on me. I asked him to come in.

problem: "My father, indeed, imposed [most editions: opposed] the determination, but since his death, I have not a legitimate obstacle" — the father was the obstacle to St. John's missionary plan; "reinforced the decision" reverses the meaning and contradicts the next clause.
new_text: "A missionary I resolved to be. From that moment my state of mind changed; the chains dissolved and fell from every faculty, leaving only their painful marks—which only time can heal. My father, it is true, opposed the decision, but since his death I have no legitimate obstacle left to contend with; some affairs to settle, a successor for Morton to arrange, an attachment or two of the heart to break through or cut away—a last conflict with human weakness, which I know I shall win because I have vowed that I will win—and I leave Europe for the East."

problem: "forgetting her usual stinted step-mother dole of gifts, had endowed this, her darling, with a grand-dame's bounty" — the stepmother/grandmother contrast is half lost ("stingy allotment").
new_text: It was true. Though Mr. Rivers had started at the first of those musical tones as if lightning had split a cloud over his head, he still stood, at the end of her sentence, in the same position she had caught him in—his arm resting on the gate, his face turned toward the west. He turned at last, with measured deliberation. A vision, it seemed to me, had appeared at his side. There stood, within three feet of him, a figure dressed in pure white—a youthful, graceful form: full yet fine in outline; and when, after stooping to pet Carlo, she raised her head and threw back a long veil, there bloomed under his gaze a face of perfect beauty. Perfect beauty is a bold claim; but I do not take it back or soften it: features as sweet as any ever shaped by England's temperate climate; colors of rose and lily as pure as any her misty skies and damp breezes ever produced—these justified the term in this case. No charm was missing, no flaw was visible; the young woman had regular, delicate features; eyes shaped and colored like those in beautiful paintings—large, dark, and full; the long, shadowy lash that frames a fine eye with such soft allure; the finely drawn brow that gives such clarity; the white, smooth forehead that adds such calm to the livelier beauties of color and light; the cheek, oval, fresh, and smooth; the lips, fresh too, rosy, healthy, sweetly shaped; the even, gleaming teeth without a flaw; the small dimpled chin; the crowning glory of rich, abundant hair—every advantage, in short, which, combined, embodies the ideal of beauty, was fully hers. I gazed at this lovely creature in wonder: I admired her with my whole heart. Nature had surely formed her in a generous mood; and, forgetting her usual stingy stepmother's handout of gifts, had showered this favorite child with a grandmother's bounty.

problem: "the Peri" (a beautiful fairy spirit of Persian legend, the image Jane uses for Rosamond) is replaced by the generic "the vision"; the allusion should remain recognizable.
new_text: What did St. John Rivers think of this earthly angel? I naturally asked myself that question as I saw him turn to her and look at her; and naturally I sought the answer in his expression. He had already withdrawn his eyes from the Peri—this fairy vision— and was staring at a humble tuft of daisies growing by the gate.

problem: "he looked nearly as beautiful for a man as she for a woman" is rendered as a garbled comparison ("as beautiful as a man can be, as she was as a woman").
new_text: As she stroked the dog's head, bending with natural grace before his young and severe master, I saw a flush rise to that master's face. I saw his solemn eye soften with sudden fire and flicker with irresistible emotion. Lit up like this, he looked nearly as beautiful for a man as she did for a woman. His chest rose once, as if his large heart, weary of its iron restraint, had swelled in spite of his will and made a powerful leap for freedom. But he checked it, I think, as a determined rider would check a rearing horse. He responded with neither word nor movement to the gentle advances she made.

problem: "good reasons to be indisposed for joining in my chatter" — the reference to her own chatter (her self-reproach) is dropped; "in low spirits" loses it.
new_text: "I forgot!" she exclaimed, shaking her beautiful curled head as if shocked at herself. "I am so giddy and thoughtless! Do excuse me. It slipped my mind that you have good reasons not to feel like joining in my chatter. Diana and Mary have left you, and Moor House is shut up, and you are so lonely. I am sure I pity you. Do come and see Papa."
